lines.cap: **Narrator:** Tuesday. Room 8H. Mock reading papers have just come back.
**Narrator:** Mr Hargreaves is on mug twenty. Something on his desk is crying.
**Question 4:** Nobody reads me! They read my first four words, panic, and start copying paragraph six!
**Mei:** Sir... why is **Question 4** sobbing on my curry puff napkin?
**Mr H:** Because I wrote '**From lines 10 to 18, explain in your own words**', and half the class quoted line thirty-two.
**Mei:** Line thirty-two was a really good quote!
**Question 4:** Wrong lines score **zero**! And you copied the text word for word! Look at my bold print: **OWN. WORDS.**
**Will:** Worse! The unseen extract was an article about Singapore **otters**. Where were the kings? Where were the **iambs**?
**Nib:** Unseen **comprehension**, Will. Reading closely under pressure. Currently, Mei gives it **one star**.
**Mei:** Unfair! How am I supposed to know what the examiner wants?
**Question 4:** I LITERALLY TELL YOU IN THE QUESTION!
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode thirteen: Read the Question.

chapters.title: Decode the question and beat the clock

lines.cap: **Question 4:** Right. Look at me properly. Every question gives you **three clues** before you write a word.
**Mr H:** Clue one: **where to look**, like lines 10 to 18. Clue two: the **command word**. Clue three: the **marks**.
**Nib:** Every paper is built from **seven question types**. Learn the mnemonic: **R**eally **I**nquisitive **V**ictors **L**ove **S**olving **S**neaky **E**xams.
**Question 4:** **Retrieval**: find facts on the surface. **Inference**: read between the lines. **Vocabulary**: explain a word in context.
**Question 4:** **Language**: how words create effects. **Structure**: how the text is ordered. **Summary**: condense in your own words. **Evaluation**: judge how far you agree.
**Mr H:** And **marks map to points**. Two marks? Give two brief points. Six marks for language? About **three developed points**.
**Mei:** Okay, so I read every single word of the passage three times first?
**Mr H:** No! Change gears. First, **skim** for the **gist**: title, opening, ending and first lines, to see what it's about.
**Nib:** Second, **scan** for a target: sweep your eyes in tiny leaps called **saccades** to spot a date, name or number.
**Mr H:** Third, **close-read** the named lines slowly for analysis, pencil in hand.
**Kevin:** Watch the clock! Spend ten minutes reading, then **a mark a minute, a point per mark**!
**Question 4:** Spend ten minutes polishing a two-mark question and you'll run out of time on Question eight. Don't break my heart.

chapters.title: On the lines and between them

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Wednesday, the library. Question 4 has called in a specialist.
**Sherlock:** Sherlock. Magnifying glass. **Retrieval** finds what is **explicit** — written plainly on the lines.
**Sherlock:** Watch out for nearby traps. In **Monsoon**, Mei's mother told her to be home by **five**. 'Ten past' is the time **now**.
**Question 4:** And if I say **in your own words**, you must **paraphrase**. Never copy the writer's key phrase!
**Mei:** The otter article says the Singapore River was 'an open sewer'. Can I write 'an uncovered sewer'?
**Question 4:** BANNED! Reword the whole idea: **so polluted with waste that almost nothing could live in it**.
**Sherlock:** Now **inference**: working out what is **implicit** — suggested between the lines.
**Mei:** Oh, so guessing! Maybe Mei's brother Wei Jie was kidnapped by space pirates!
**Nib:** Space pirates?! Inference is **deduction from textual clues**, darling, never wild invention.
**Sherlock:** Look at Dickens on **Scrooge**: even **blind men's dogs** tugged their owners into doorways when he approached.
**Mr H:** **Point**: everyone dreads Scrooge. **Evidence**: 'tug their owners into doorways'. **Explain**: even animals sense his cruelty.
**Will:** Or Captain Oates in Scott's **1912** journal, walking into a blizzard: 'I am just going outside and may be some time.'
**Nib:** **Understatement**. Casual words hide deliberate self-sacrifice. We infer his courage from what he leaves unsaid.
**Sherlock:** Same trick for **vocabulary in context**. Jack London writes: 'an intangible **pall** over the face of things, a subtle gloom'.
**Mr H:** The phrase next door explains the **denotation**: a dark covering. Its **connotation** — a cloth over a coffin — hints at **death**.
**Narrator:** Thursday. Mei is tackling a six-mark language question on Scrooge.
**Mei:** 'Dickens uses a simile, solitary as an oyster, to create a vivid image and make the reader want to read on.' Done!
**Nib:** My nib! I am leaking! '**Makes the reader want to read on**' says NOTHING! Every writer wants you to read on!
**Mr H:** Use **What, How, Why**. **What**: a short embedded quote. **How**: the technique or word class. **Why**: the precise **effect**.
**Question 4:** The **Why** is where my marks live! Spotting 'simile' without explaining its effect is just **feature-spotting**.
**Will:** Unpack Dickens's simile: '**solitary as an oyster**'. What is an oyster like, child?
**Mei:** Hard, rough shell... clamped tightly shut! So Scrooge locks himself away from human warmth.
**Will:** Aye! And **alternatively**, what hides inside an oyster? A **pearl** — hinting something precious still lies buried within him.
**Nib:** **Zoom in** on single words. Dickens writes that Scrooge's inner cold '**nipped** his pointed nose'.
**Mei:** The verb '**nipped**' means pinched or bitten — like frostbite, and like a miser **pinching** every penny!
**Nib:** Then **zoom out** to patterns: the **present participles** 'squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching' pile up relentlessly.
**Mr H:** And across the whole paragraph, frost, ice and winter form an **extended metaphor** of emotional coldness.
**Mei:** Two stars. The pearl inside the oyster actually blew my mind.
**Question 4:** Warning! Question five says: **How has the writer structured the text to interest the reader?**
**Mei:** Easy! 'The writer uses paragraphs and punctuation, and also the metaphor silver curtain—'
**Question 4:** STOP! 'Silver curtain' is **language**! Analysing metaphors in a **structure** question scores zero!
**Mr H:** Language is the **words**. Structure is the **architecture**: order, focus, pace, openings and endings.
**Will:** Look at how Dickens opens: '**Marley was dead: to begin with.**' A blunt shock — then 'to begin with' **foreshadows** a ghost!
**Sherlock:** Track the text like a **camera** from start to middle to end. Watch the passage **Monsoon**.
**Mr H:** **At the start**, a **wide shot**: the whole sky over Toa Payoh holding its breath, establishing tension.
**Nib:** **In the middle**, the focus narrows to Mei waiting, with **foreshadowing**: Wei Jie never broke a promise — 'not until today'.
**Mr H:** Then a **close-up**: one fat raindrop landing on her wrist. Followed by a tiny **one-line paragraph**.
**Mei:** '**Then another. Then a thousand.**' Two short **minor sentences** speed up the **pace** as the storm explodes!
**Kevin:** And nobody put me between them! Thank goodness! Two separate punches, not a comma splice!
**Sherlock:** **By the end**, one isolated line: '**It was not Wei Jie.**' A **cliffhanger** shifting tension from storm to stranger.
**Nib:** And if an ending echoes the opening — like the stubborn key in **Number 47** — call it a **cyclical structure**.
**Narrator:** Friday. Non-fiction, summary and the big ten-mark evaluation question.
**Mr H:** For **non-fiction** — articles, journals, speeches, travel writing — spot **form**, **audience**, **purpose** and **viewpoint**.
**Sherlock:** Separate **fact** from **opinion**: **Check it or Challenge it**. 'In **1977** the clean-up began' — you can **check** it. Fact!
**Mei:** 'Otters are the **best news** our city has had in years' — someone with a koi pond could **challenge** 'best'. Opinion!
**Nib:** Even if everyone agrees with Scott calling the South Pole 'an **awful** place', 'awful' is still a **judgement**, so it's an **opinion**.
**Question 4:** For a **summary**: select relevant points, condense them **in your own words**, one point per mark. **No quotes, no language analysis!**
**Mr H:** Finally, **evaluation**: '**How far do you agree?**' Those words '**how far**' are a gift — weigh **both** sides.
**Question 4:** Statement: 'Scott's journal is as much a **public message** as a **private diary**.' Climb the ladder, Mei!
**Mei:** **Verdict**: I **largely agree** — it begins as a private log, yet is shaped for the nation to read.
**Mei:** **Counter-view**: dated entries about gale winds and '**two cups of tea**' feel like practical survival notes.
**Mei:** **Evidence for**: **However**, 'Should this be found' and praising Oates as 'an **English gentleman**' address future readers.
**Mei:** **Link**: knowing '**our dead bodies must tell the tale**', Scott turns a tent diary into public testimony.
**Question 4:** She read the question! She weighed both sides! These are **happy** tears! Full marks!
**Narrator:** Before the bell, Room 8H's mark-saving checklist.
**Mei:** Memory hooks! Seven types: **Really Inquisitive Victors Love Solving Sneaky Exams**. Analysis: **What, How, Why**. Timing: **a mark a minute**. Facts: **Check it or Challenge it**.
**Question 4:** One. Stay inside the **line numbers**! Evidence from the wrong paragraph scores **nothing**.
**Nib:** Two. Never **feature-spot** or write 'makes the reader want to read on'. Marks come from the **specific effect**.
**Sherlock:** Three. '**In your own words**' means genuine paraphrase — never recycle the writer's key words, and never guess without clues.
**Mr H:** Four. In a **structure** question, track shifts in focus, zoom and pace — don't analyse metaphors or retell the plot.
**Kevin:** Five. In a **summary**, no quotations and no language analysis! And watch the clock on one-mark questions!
**Will:** Six. On '**How far do you agree?**', give a clear verdict like '**I largely agree, although...**' and include a counter-view.
**Mei:** Reading Comprehension: **four stars**. Way easier once you actually read the question.
**Question 4:** Four stars out of five?! Show your evidence!
**Mei:** The passages are a bit long, lah.
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** What is the difference between **skimming** and **scanning**?
**Mei:** **Skimming** reads quickly for the overall **gist**; **scanning** hunts for one **specific detail**.
**Mr H:** A question asks what a character's behaviour **suggests**. Which question type is that?
**Sherlock:** **Inference** — reading between the lines using **clues** from the text.
**Mr H:** In Jack London's phrase 'an intangible **pall**', what does **pall** connote beyond darkness?
**Nib:** **Death and funerals** — a pall is the cloth laid over a coffin, foreshadowing danger.
**Mr H:** Why does a **one-line paragraph** like 'It was not Wei Jie.' count as **structure**?
**Question 4:** Because isolating a short sentence controls **pace** and **focus**, ending on a **cliffhanger**.
**Mr H:** Is 'This is an **awful** place' a **fact** or an **opinion**?
**Kevin:** An **opinion**! Even if everyone agrees, '**awful**' is a judgement you can challenge, not check.
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **Reading Comprehension** quiz in your English Lab.
**Question 4:** And read every word of the question before you click!
**Will:** Especially if it's about me.
